Need to search first.I've got notes for most verses in 1 Samuel 17:1–29, but the research is incomplete. The search tool hit its usage limit early and the page fetches didn't work. So everything below comes from search-result excerpts of each page, not full readings. Several sources you asked for are missing (see the end), and parts 2 and 3 are thin. Everything is in my own words, with the URL after each point.

**Translation note for v. 29:** The commentators work from the KJV/NKJV wording, "Is there not a cause?" The BSB has "Was it not just a question?" Their comments on this verse depend on the older wording.

---

## 1. Traditional reading, verse by verse

**v. 1**
- Ellicott places the site about 12–15 miles southwest of Jerusalem and 9–10 miles from Bethlehem, Jesse's home. He reads the name Ephes-dammim, "boundary of blood," as a sign of constant border fighting there. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-17.html
- Gill says 1 Chronicles 11:13 shortens the name to Pasdammim. He reports a Jewish tradition that the place got its name because "there blood ceased." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-17.html
- Precept Austin points out that the Philistines are the attackers. It traces this war back to Saul's earlier failures: his foolish oath and his decision not to chase the Philistines (1 Sam 14). That is why war with them was "severe all the days of Saul" (14:52). It adds that God uses this consequence of Saul's sin to raise David up. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-17-commentary
- Matthew Henry thinks the Philistines had probably heard that Samuel had left Saul and that Saul had become gloomy and unfit to lead, and took their chance. His lesson: the church's enemies have their best opening when its protectors have driven away God's Spirit and prophets. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Sa/1Sa_017.cfm

**v. 2**
- Gill quotes a traveller who describes the "valley of Terebinth" as small but famous as the place where Goliath was killed. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-17.html
- Precept Austin says the valley is named after its large, shady terebinth trees. It describes a huge old terebinth near Shochoh, and nearby sites (Azekah, Socoh, Adullam, and Khirbet Qeiyafa, identified with Sha'araim in v. 52). https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-17-commentary

**v. 3**
- Precept Austin says the battle lines between God's people and God's enemies were clearly drawn here, with "no gray area." https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/64001/

**v. 4**
- Guzik (Enduring Word) puts "six cubits and a span" at roughly 8'5" to 9'2", with armour and weapons to match. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-17/
- Guzik's study guide cites Adam Clarke: the Hebrew word for "champion" means "a middle man," the man who stands between two armies and fights for his side. https://blueletterbible.org/Comm/guzik_david/StudyGuide2017-1Sa/1Sa-17.cfm
- Gill, Ellicott and Matthew Henry all link Goliath to the Anakim, the race of giants left in Gath in Joshua's day (Josh 11:22). Henry suggests Goliath was probably one of the largest of them.
  - Gill: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-17.html
  - Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/17.htm
  - Henry: https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-samuel/17-6.html
- Gill also notes the reading of four cubits and a span (about eight feet), which Josephus follows. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-17.html
- Bible Hub's verse notes treat the height (about 9'9") as literal, not figurative. They draw the lesson that victory depends on the LORD, not human strength (Deut 20:4; Ps 33:16–17). https://biblehub.com/1_samuel/17-4.htm

**vv. 5–6**
- GotQuestions, quoted on Precept Austin, puts the bronze armour at about 125 pounds. Precept Austin also gives a scholar's estimate of about 126 pounds, and describes bronze leg armour (greaves) tied around the calves. Its point: however big Goliath looks, he is small next to the living God. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/64001/
- Same point from GotQuestions directly: https://www.gotquestions.org/how-tall-was-Goliath.html

**v. 7**
- Gill says the wooden shaft was as thick as the beam of a weaver's loom. He reckons that, in proportion to Goliath's size, the spear could have been about 26 feet long, comparing Hector's spear in Homer. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-17.html
- GotQuestions, quoted on Precept Austin, gives the spearhead as about 15 pounds. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/64001/

**vv. 8–10**
- Guzik calls this a bold challenge. He stresses that the fight was representative: whatever happened to each champion would happen to his whole people. He later builds a picture of Christ on this point (see v. 17). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-17/
- Matthew Henry, citing Bishop Patrick, thinks the offer was only bluster. No nation would really stake everything on one man. In fact the Philistines did not keep the terms after Goliath died. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Sa/1Sa_017.cfm

**v. 11**
- Guzik says fear was exactly what Goliath wanted. He "defeated the Israelites with fear alone." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-17/
- Matthew Henry says the people lost heart because they saw Saul's courage fail. If the leader is a coward, you can't expect the followers to be bold. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Sa/1Sa_017.cfm
- Precept Austin includes a comment asking why Jonathan, so brave earlier, didn't step forward. Its answer: God had not stirred him to it this time, and the honour was saved for David. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-17-commentary

**v. 12**
- Bible Hub notes that Bethlehem means "house of bread." https://biblehub.com/chaptersummaries/1_samuel/17.htm

**vv. 13–15**
- Guzik thinks David was called to the palace only when needed, when Saul's distressing spirit troubled him. He suggests this may help explain why Saul later doesn't seem to recognise David (vv. 55–58). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-17/
- Precept Austin says Jesse was too old and David too young to serve in the army. It finds this surprising, since 16:18 already called David "a mighty man of valor." https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-17-commentary

**v. 16**
- Guzik notes that Saul had waited at least 40 days for anyone to volunteer. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-17/

**vv. 17–18**
- Matthew Henry says Jesse wanted to know whether his sons were short of food in a long campaign. "Bring back an assurance" may mean redeeming anything they had pawned, or checking what company they kept. He compares Joseph reporting on his brothers. His lesson: children away from their parents' eyes are still under God's eye. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Sa/1Sa_017.cfm
- Guzik treats the whole episode as a picture of Christ: both David and Jesus were sent to the battle by their father. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-17/

**v. 19**
- Ellicott reads this verse as the end of Jesse's instructions (telling David where to find his brothers), not as the narrator's aside. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-17.html
- Precept Austin says there was no actual fighting yet. The only "fighting" was Goliath's daily taunts. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-17-commentary

**vv. 20–21**
- Guzik suggests this scene of marching out and shouting had probably repeated itself for 40 days. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/1-samuel/1-samuel-17.cfm

**v. 23**
- Gill describes Goliath coming up out of the valley toward the hill the Israelites were coming down. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-17.html
- Ellicott flags a difficulty: 2 Samuel 21:19 says Elhanan of Bethlehem killed "Goliath of Gath" after David became king. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/17.htm

**v. 24**
- Precept Austin says David was shocked to find Israel's army cowering in fear. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-17-commentary

**v. 25**
- Ellicott counts tax freedom for the winner's family among Saul's lavish offers. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/17.htm
- Guzik notes that the other soldiers thought about the reward or the danger. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-17/

**v. 26**
- Guzik: David alone saw the problem in spiritual terms. The giant had defied the armies of the living God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-17/
- Matthew Henry gives two reasons for David's holy anger:
  - Goliath was uncircumcised, outside God's covenant.
  - Israel's armies belonged to the living God, so the insult was really against God.

  Henry also notes that when David later speaks to Saul, he doesn't mention the reward at all. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Sa/1Sa_017.cfm
- Ellicott pictures the shepherd boy, "glowing with religious fervour," going from group to group of gloomy soldiers and asking about the man insulting his God. He stresses this was no mere duel: the nation's future was at stake. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/17.htm

**v. 28**
- Matthew Henry: Eliab's outburst came from jealousy. Perhaps he was used to bullying his youngest brother. Henry calls the charge baseless, since David was known for humility, and he warns that proud elder brothers may yet see the younger exalted. Those who take on great work should expect scorn even from friends. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Sa/1Sa_017.cfm
- Precept Austin compares Eliab to Jesus' relatives who misunderstood him. It says Eliab's reaction confirms God's wisdom in choosing David over him (ch. 16), and that it was also an insult to their father, who had sent David. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-17-commentary
- Ellicott reports a commentator (not named in the excerpt) who completes the David–Christ parallel: David, sent by his father on an errand of kindness, was badly received by his brothers, as Christ was by the Jews. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/17.htm

**v. 29**
- Guzik: Eliab's words hurt David, but David would not let them stop him. He put God's cause ahead of his own feelings. Guzik says this is where the battle was really won: had David answered in the flesh, he would have lost his strength. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-17/
- Matthew Henry reads "Is there not a cause?" two ways: his father sent him, and Israel's honour had been insulted. David gave a soft answer instead of trading insults. Henry calls this victory over his own temper in some ways more honourable than killing Goliath. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Sa/1Sa_017.cfm

## 2. Differences between Protestant traditions

I couldn't find sources comparing Baptist, Methodist, Pentecostal, Reformed, Lutheran or Anglican readings of this passage. The searches ran out before I reached those sites. The only difference visible is in how much is made of David as a picture of Christ:
- **Gaebelein** (a dispensational Bible teacher, Plymouth Brethren in background) reads it fully symbolically:
  - Goliath stands for Satan, and his measurements recall the 666 of Revelation.
  - "Ephes-dammim" and "Elah" stand for blood and power, death and resurrection.

  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gab/1-samuel-17.html
- **Guzik** (Calvary Chapel) makes a more limited comparison of David and Jesus: both represented their people, were sent by their father, and were rejected by their brothers. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-17/

## 3. Other views

- **v. 4, Goliath's height (text-critical):** The Hebrew (Masoretic) text says six cubits and a span. The Greek Septuagint says four cubits and a span, and the NET Bible follows the shorter height ("close to seven feet").
  - GotQuestions: https://www.gotquestions.org/how-tall-was-Goliath.html
  - The BSB footnote says the Septuagint, the Dead Sea Scrolls and Josephus all read four cubits (about 6'9"): https://biblehub.com/chaptersummaries/1_samuel/17.htm
  - Brenton's English Septuagint shows "four cubits and a span": https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/dby/1-samuel/17-4.html
- **v. 23 and 2 Samuel 21:19:** The "who killed Goliath" difficulty above. Bible Hub's cross-reference shows the BSB rendering of 2 Sam 21:19 as Elhanan killing "the brother of Goliath." https://biblehub.com/1_samuel/17-4.htm

**Not found:** the Pulpit Commentary, the NET Bible notes themselves, Bible Odyssey, Catholic and Orthodox readings, specific Protestant traditions, and popular modern teaching (prosperity, word of faith, hyper-grace). I've left these out rather than guess. Running these searches again when the tool limit resets would fill the gaps.
